creative.body:
I used to spend $340 a month on Miralax, fiber powders, and probiotics that did nothing.

That was just 1 month. My daughter is an accountant. She made me total up 3 years of receipts at my kitchen table on a Sunday afternoon.

The number was $4,217.

I'm going to tell you what that $4,217 actually bought me, what it almost cost me on top of the money, and what finally broke the cycle after 3 years of standing in the laxative aisle every Tuesday night convinced that the next bottle was going to be the one.

Because the part nobody told me, and the part I'm telling you now, is that the longer you keep paying into the wrong aisle, the harder it gets to even believe a real answer exists.

I'm 67. I have 3 grandchildren. By the time my daughter forced me to add up that shoebox, I had been chronically constipated for 3 years. 7 days. 9 days. Once, 11. The bloat would set in by 3 PM every afternoon and by dinner I was wearing my husband's t-shirts because nothing of mine fit around the middle anymore.

The shoebox itself was almost worse than the constipation.

Miralax at $28 a bottle, gone in 10 days. Some weeks I went through 3 bottles. Metamucil at $19 a tub, every flavor they made. 3 different probiotics rotated like I was searching for a magic strain, $40 each, sometimes 2 going at once. Magnesium citrate that tastes like salty lemon despair. Senna tea. Prune juice by the case from Costco. 2 GI co-pays a year at $80. A colonoscopy that came back completely normal and somehow still cost me $340 out of pocket. A 21-day "gut reset" cleanse my friend swore by, $189, gave me cramps and nothing else.

By month 6 I had a wire shelving unit installed in my bathroom cabinet just to organize all the products I was failing with.

I stood in the laxative aisle at Walgreens on a Tuesday night in October trying to choose between Dulcolax and a stronger senna and I realized I had no idea why I was there. I'd already tried 8 things. None of them worked. I was just buying a 9th one because I didn't know what else to do.

That was the moment it stopped being frustrating and started being something else.

I wasn't confused anymore. I was exhausted.

My husband asked me one night if I'd eaten dinner and I said yes. I hadn't. I'd stopped eating full meals because the pressure under my ribs was unbearable by evening. I'm a 67-year-old grandmother and I was skipping dinner in my own kitchen, hiding it from the man I'd been married to for 41 years, because the alternative was 3 days of bloating I couldn't face.

That same week my granddaughter came into the kitchen for water and saw me at the table not eating and she asked, "Grandma, are you sick?"

I told her no.

But I sat there after she went back upstairs and I thought about how to answer that question honestly. I had a cabinet full of products that were supposed to be helping. A wire shelf full. $4,217 worth. And the 9-year-old at my kitchen table could see what 4 doctors hadn't.

The Sunday after Thanksgiving my daughter brought her laptop over and she made me do it. The receipts. CVS. Walgreens. Amazon order history going back to 2023. Insurance portal printouts. The cleanse kit invoice.

When the spreadsheet hit $4,217 I cried at the table. Not because of the money. We're comfortable. We can afford it.

I cried because every line item was me believing, one more time, that this would be the thing. And every single time I was wrong.

I went back to my GP that week. Dr. Reynolds. I've known him 15 years. I laid out the spreadsheet, the bottles, the lying about dinner, the granddaughter.

He listened. Then he said something I hadn't heard from any of my other doctors.

"Joan, all of those products work on your colon. Your problem isn't in your colon."

He said it in the same flat tone he'd ask me about my blood pressure. Like it should have been obvious. Like every other doctor I'd seen should have already told me.

None of them had.

He explained that for women my age, the bowel issue almost always starts higher up. In the stomach itself. If the stomach gets sluggish, food sits there and ferments. The fermentation creates the gas, the pressure, the 3 PM bloat. By the time anything reaches the colon the whole system is already overwhelmed.

You can pour all the Miralax in the world into a system like that. You're trying to flush a sink while the faucet upstairs is barely dripping.

I asked him why nobody had ever told me this in 3 years.

He paused.

"Because the products that target it aren't pharmaceuticals. They don't get advertised on television. Most patients walk in with constipation and walk out with another laxative."

Then he said the part that stayed with me on the drive home.

"I have a patient who waited 6 years before anyone told her this. Her stomach motility is permanently compromised now. We're managing it. We can't reverse it. Don't wait."

I sat in my car in the parking lot for a long time after that.

That night I sat at my kitchen table with my iPad and I searched, for the first time in 3 years, not "best laxative for older women." I searched "why does the stomach slow down after 60."

For the first time I wasn't looking for a product. I was looking for an explanation.

Until almost 2 AM I read about a compound called apigenin. Concentrated in celery. Acts as a natural prokinetic, helping the smooth muscle of the stomach start contracting again. The actual part that slows down with age. While food is sitting up there fermenting, sulfur gas builds up. So the second piece I found was chlorophyllin, which binds those sulfur compounds. And the third piece, once the stomach is moving and the gas is handled, is a soluble prebiotic fiber, the gentle kind that feeds the good bacteria already living in your gut so the rest of the system is ready when food finally moves through.

I went back to my bathroom and looked at every bottle on the wire shelves.

Not 1 of them did the first 2 things.

I didn't know what to do with that. I wasn't going to walk into Walgreens and ask the pharmacist for "standardized apigenin extract." I'd already learned the hard way that the loudest bottle on the shelf is almost never the right one.

So I sat with it. For about 2 weeks I kept the printed pages from that 2 AM research session in a folder on my kitchen counter and every time I reached for a Miralax bottle I read them again.

It was the second Saturday in December at my granddaughter's piano recital that the answer finally walked into my life.

I ended up sitting next to another grandmother in the second row. Older than me by a few years. We'd nodded at each other before. I knew she was a retired pharmacist from a compounding lab over in Tucson.

I don't know why but I told her. About the 3 years. About the wire shelves. About the $4,217 spreadsheet. About the granddaughter at the kitchen table asking if I was sick.

She was quiet for a second and then she said something I didn't expect.

"My older sister had her stomach motility shut down from years on a different medication and she never got it fully back. After she died, I went through every supplement on the market that claimed to help with the upper digestive tract. Most of them are fillers. A few of them are real."

I asked her how she knew which ones were real.

She told me she'd had a colleague at her old lab run third-party assays on 22 of the most popular celery and apigenin supplements on the market.

18 came in under 5 milligrams of standardized apigenin per serving. 5 had heavy metal contamination above safe limits. 3 had no detectable apigenin at all. Just rice powder and gelatin.

Only 2 products consistently tested at clinical-grade apigenin concentration.

She told me 1 of them was a small company called Motilli. A heart-shaped gummy specifically formulated for older women whose stomach motility had slowed with age. Standardized apigenin extract from celery, not powder. Combined with chlorophyllin for the sulfur gas and a soluble prebiotic for the downstream support.

She said her own younger sister, 64, had been on it for 5 months. Bloating gone. Bathroom mornings normal. Eating full dinners with her husband again.

"She's the reason I tested everything else. I needed to know there was nothing better. There isn't."

I asked her where to get it. She pulled out her phone right there in the recital hall and sent me the link before my granddaughter walked back on stage.

I ordered 1 bottle that night.

The first 4 days, nothing.

Day 5, the bloating was less intense by evening. Not gone. Less. I didn't think much of it.

Day 7, my husband mentioned at dinner that I looked less puffy. He said my face looked "normal again." I didn't know what to do with that.

Day 9, I went. On my own. No Miralax. No magnesium the night before. I just woke up and went. I sat there for a second afterward because I honestly couldn't remember the last time that had happened without me forcing it.

Day 14, I ate a full plate of my husband's pasta with our nephew who was visiting from Phoenix. 3 hours later I was on the couch laughing at a movie and I realized I hadn't thought about my stomach once.

Week 3, my granddaughter was over on a Saturday. We made cookies. I ate 2. She didn't ask me if I was sick this time.

The Saturday after week 4, I went to the bathroom cabinet and I got a trash bag and I swept everything in. The half-empty Miralax. The 2 tubs of Metamucil. The 4 probiotic bottles. The senna. The unfinished cleanse. The wire shelves came out next.

My husband watched me carry it to the garage and said, "Took you long enough."

My sister Marlene started taking it in February. She's 65. Same laxative graveyard. She called me after 2 weeks and said, "I don't understand how this is different from everything else I've tried."

I told her what Dr. Reynolds told me. It's not working on your colon. It's working on your stomach. That's why it's different.

I walked past the laxative aisle at Walgreens last week. Didn't stop. Didn't even slow down.

That aisle owned me for 3 years and $4,217. Every Tuesday or Wednesday I'd be standing there reading boxes trying to figure out which 1 would be the 1 that finally worked.

They all worked. They all did exactly what they were supposed to do.

They just did it to the wrong organ.

I'm a 67-year-old woman who spent $4,217 on products that couldn't have helped me because they weren't designed for the problem I actually had.

If you have your own version of that wire shelf, and you're rotating through laxatives and probiotics and fiber and none of them are doing anything, it's not the products. It's not you. It's that the problem is in your stomach and everything in your cabinet works on your colon.

And if you've already figured that part out and you're about to grab whatever celery capsule comes up first online, please pause. Standardized apigenin extract is not the same thing as ground-up celery in a pill. Most of what's on the market is the latter. Another month on the wrong dose is another month you don't get back.

There are 2 versions of the next 90 days for you.

In 1 of them, you keep adding to the shoebox. Another bottle of Miralax, another tub of fiber, another generic celery capsule, another co-pay. You skip dinner and lie to your husband about it. You wait for it to "get better on its own" the way I waited for 3 years and the way the woman Dr. Reynolds told me about waited for 6.

In the other one, you stop paying into the wrong aisle, you give your stomach the actual compound it has been asking for in the actual form your body can absorb, and you watch what happens between week 1 and week 6.

That is the whole choice.

The link is below if you want it.

A few notes on what to expect.

They run a 90-day money-back guarantee on it, which is the only reason I tried it after I'd been burned 9 times already. Anyone who has been handed another laxative for 3 years deserves to find out for themselves without losing anything else.

They batch-produce in small quantities because apigenin degrades when it's exposed to light and heat for too long. The bottles sell out for stretches when older women find them through their daughters and their book clubs and their granddaughters' piano recitals the way I did. If you go to the link and the bottle is in stock, I would not wait until next week.

I'm not going to promise you what I can't. I'm going to tell you what happened to me. I went from a $4,217 shoebox and a 9-year-old asking if I was sick, to making cookies on a Saturday morning and not noticing my stomach.

That took 6 weeks.

If you've already given 3 years and 4 grand to the wrong aisle, 6 weeks on the right one is the trade I would make every time.

P.S. The pharmacist from the recital. I sat next to her again this past Saturday at another one of my granddaughter's recitals and I tried to thank her. She waved me off and said her older sister, the one who never got her stomach back, was the only reason she ever knew which bottle to recommend. She said, "I couldn't save her. But every woman I hand that link to is somebody I might." I keep thinking about that. We never know whose answer we're going to be. The link is below.
